h: Music in a venue is licensed several times over. Here is how it works in the US.
t: Playing recorded or live music in a business is a public performance. In the US, songwriters are paid through performing rights organizations (PROs), mainly ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR. Each licenses only the works of its own members, so one license does not cover another’s songs. A business music service generally covers only the recorded music it supplies, not your band, DJ or karaoke night. - ASCAP its members’ songs only - BMI its members’ songs only - SESAC its members’ songs only - GMR its members’ songs only - and your music service recorded background music only Five separate sources of permission. A gap in any one is a gap in your coverage. - $4,500 a year on average: what the National Restaurant Association says its members pay to license music. - ~200% rise in per-hotel PRO fees from 2021 to 2025 at one unnamed global chain, as cited by the American Hotel & Lodging Association. Where a song is played without the right license, US law allows statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per work, and up to $150,000 if a court finds the infringement willful. h: Got a letter from BMI, ASCAP, SESAC or GMR?
t: It is real, it is common, and a first letter does not usually go away on its own. Here is what it means and what to do this week. On this page What it isThis weekWhat to avoidHelp

Performing rights organizations (PROs) license the public performance of songs for songwriters and publishers. Bars, restaurants and hotels are among the businesses that take PRO licenses (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR each represent their own members’ works, so a venue can need more than one license (SESAC, “What is a performing rights organization?”). A first letter usually offers a license and asks about your venue. Some go on to follow-up contact. In October 2026, music publishers and songwriters affiliated with ASCAP filed copyright infringement lawsuits against hospitality and entertainment businesses in several states, and several complaints reportedly allege repeated licensing contact before suit (Brownstein client alert, “Music licensing under the microscope” (Nov. 9, 2026)). For each work infringed, a court may award statutory damages of $750 to $30,000, up to $150,000 if the infringement is willful, and as little as $200 if the infringer proves it was innocent (17 U.S.C. §504(c), statutory damages). That is the range the law allows, not a prediction for your venue.

- Note the deadline and who sent it. Check that it is a genuine PRO. - List every music use : background music source, live music, DJs, karaoke, TVs, events, social videos. - Gather what you already pay : music service contract and any PRO invoices. - Check your music service terms. Some services state that their license covers the recorded music they supply, and not live bands, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). - Check the small-business exemption if you only play radio or TV broadcasts (see the rules). - Reply on time, with facts. If the letter mentions a lawsuit or comes from a lawyer, talk to a US attorney first.

- Ignoring it. Several lawsuit complaints reportedly describe repeated contact before filing (Brownstein client alert, “Music licensing under the microscope” (Nov. 9, 2026)), so silence tends to prolong the matter rather than end it. - Assuming your music service covers live performances. Services generally cover their own recorded catalog, not live bands, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). - Assuming one PRO license covers everything. Each PRO licenses its own members’ works. - Switching to a personal streaming account. Spotify’s terms grant “personal, non-commercial use” (Spotify End User Agreement, section 3).

h: Why a personal account is not enough
t: The terms of the big consumer services limit use to personal listening: - Spotify grants permission for “personal, non-commercial use” (Spotify End User Agreement, section 3). - Apple allows use of its services and content “only for personal, noncommercial purposes” (Apple Media Services Terms, section F). - YouTube’s terms say you may listen to content for personal, non-commercial use, and that you may not publicly screen videos or stream music from the service (YouTube Terms of Service). Playing a personal plan to customers goes beyond those terms.

- Business music service : Published entry prices start around $15 to $25 per location per month on annual terms: Pandora CloudCover from $16.95, Mood Media from $15.30, Rockbot $25 per zone. Higher tiers cost more. Checked November 12, 2026; see the sources for current prices. A service generally covers its own recorded catalog played in public areas, not live performances, cover artists, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). - Direct PRO licenses : Venues that play music not supplied by a licensed service, or that host live music, DJs or karaoke, may need licenses from each PRO whose catalog is played (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). - Radio or TV, small venue : Certain broadcasts can be exempt in small venues, within equipment limits. h: Is my venue exempt from music licensing?
t: Possibly, but only for certain radio and TV broadcasts, and only within strict limits. On this page The ruleNever coveredNext step

17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B) exempts a business from needing a separate license to play a transmission of a nondramatic musical work that comes from an FCC-licensed radio or TV station (or, for video, a cable system or satellite carrier), if all of these hold (17 U.S.C. §110(5), exemption for certain establishments): - Food and drink venues : Under 3,750 gross square feet (excluding customer parking): no equipment limits. - Other businesses : Under 2,000 gross square feet: no equipment limits. - Larger venues : Audio on no more than 6 loudspeakers, with no more than 4 in any one room. Video on no more than 4 screens, no more than 1 per room, none larger than 55 inches diagonal. - In every case : No direct charge to see or hear the transmission; it is not transmitted further beyond the venue; and the transmission is licensed by the copyright owner.

- Streaming services, downloads, CDs or vinyl. The statute covers only broadcast and cable or satellite transmissions. - Live music, DJs or karaoke. - Music you add to social media or marketing videos. A plain-English summary of the statute for general information. Check the current text, or ask a US attorney, before relying on it. An overview is available from the Congressional Research Service, RS21107.

h: Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke?
t: Usually yes, and the four PROs all say the license sits with the venue, not with the band or the DJ. On this page Who is responsibleYour music serviceThe DJ's subscriptionWhich licensesNext step

h: The venue is responsible, not the performer
t: Each of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs) says the license for performances on your premises is the business’s responsibility: - ASCAP: “the business owner is legally responsible to obtain the license”, and its FAQ adds that live music of any kind, “including DJ nights and karaoke”, needs public performance licenses (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). - BMI: whether music is “performed by a live band, DJ or karaoke, the business owner must obtain permission from the copyright owner” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). - SESAC: “a business cannot shift its responsibility to musicians or entertainers” (SESAC, who is responsible for paying music licensing fees), and “Paying the band does not cover you” (SESAC FAQ). - GMR: the owner or operator is responsible for the performances on its premises, and paying the performers “will not relieve you of your licensing obligation” (Global Music Rights FAQ). US courts took the same view long ago. In 1929 a federal appeals court held a dance hall owner liable for songs played by a hired orchestra, “even though the orchestra be employed under a contract that would ordinarily make it an independent contractor” (Dreamland Ball Room v. Shapiro, B

h: Your background music service usually stops at background music
t: Business music services license the recorded music they supply for background use. Several say in writing that live entertainment is outside that: - Pandora CloudCover : “A background music license also does not cover live performances, cover artists, DJs”, and the music cannot be integral to the activity, such as karaoke (CloudCover licensing FAQ, updated July 2026). - Soundtrack : If a business “Plays music from another source other than the Service such as a DJ, karaoke, or live music” or “Charges an admission fee”, the public performance rights “are not licensed by Soundtrack” (Soundtrack General Terms, March 2026). - Custom Channels : “Music from DJs, live bands, karaoke, or trivia events is not covered and may require separate PRO licenses” (Custom Channels help center). The PROs describe the same limit from their side. SESAC says a service’s license “only extends to the music they supply to establishments with no admission, membership or similar charge” (SESAC FAQ). ASCAP says karaoke and DJ nights require “additional licensing by the establishment” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs).

h: The DJ’s own subscription is not your license
t: DJs often stream from a DJ service. Some of those services say plainly that the subscription does not cover playing in public: - Beatport: streamed content “is intended for your personal use only”, and public performance “will require additional licensing, which is not included as part of your subscription” (Beatport Streaming terms of use). - VirtualDJ: its Online Music membership “does not give you the right to perform music in public”, and the DJ or the venue needs the public performance licenses (VirtualDJ, Public Performance License). A clause in your booking agreement can say who handles what, but the PRO statements above put the license with the venue.

h: Which licenses a live night touches
t: A band or DJ can play songs from any catalog, and each PRO licenses only the works it represents. That is why a venue paying one or two PROs can still have gaps on live nights. Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR? explains how the four fit together, and what a license costs shows how live nights change the fee.

h: Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?
t: It depends on what you play. Each PRO licenses only its own songs, and many songs are split between several of them. On this page Each licenses its ownSplit songsHow they differLook up a songNext step

h: Each PRO licenses only its own songs
t: The four US performing rights organizations (PROs) each say the same thing about their licenses: - BMI: a license from another PRO “allows you only to perform copyrighted music represented by that organization”, because “each PRO licenses a unique repertoire of music” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). - SESAC: each organization “licenses only the copyrighted works of its own respective copyright holders” (SESAC FAQ). - GMR: licenses with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC “do not grant you authorization” to perform music by GMR’s writers, “and vice versa” (Global Music Rights FAQ). - ASCAP: “you need a license with each PRO that represents the creators of the music that you play” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). So the practical question is not “which PRO is the right one” but “whose songs are played here, and which licenses cover them”. A curated background music service changes the answer for the music it supplies; see Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar?

h: One song can need more than one license
t: Songs are often co-written by writers who belong to different PROs. The U.S. Copyright Office notes that the rights to musical works “are often split among multiple songwriters, with differing publishers and PROs” (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015), p. 123). The Department of Justice describes the result, called fractional licensing: a PRO licenses only its share of a work, “meaning that a licensee must obtain a license from all of the PROs affiliated with the work (or from the songwriters or publishers directly) in order to legally perform it” (DOJ statement closing its review of the ASCAP and BMI consent decrees (January 15, 2021), p. 2).

ASCAP and BMI operate under long-standing antitrust consent decrees with the Department of Justice; SESAC and GMR do not. The Copyright Office puts it this way: “neither SESAC nor GMR is subject to such direct antitrust regulation” (Copyright and the Music Marketplace, p. 34), and the DOJ notes the decrees “regulate only ASCAP and BMI” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2). For a venue, the day-to-day point is simpler: each sets its own fees for bars and restaurants, and each needs its own license. How much does a music license cost? explains what drives those fees.

h: Look up which PRO represents a song
t: Each PRO publishes a free search: - Songview : A shared database that BMI describes as covering “the four major PROs, BMI, ASCAP, GMR and SESAC”, with ownership shares per song (Songview at BMI; also reachable from ASCAP’s repertory search). - SESAC : SESAC repertory search: titles, SESAC’s share, and its writers and publishers. - GMR : Global Music Rights search: by title, performer, songwriter or publisher. A search tells you who represents a song, not whether your venue is licensed for it. Searching song by song is also impractical for a live band or a DJ, who can play hundreds of titles a night.

t: The audit maps what is played in your venue against the licenses you hold, catalog by catalog, and flags gaps and possible double payments. Free 2-minute checkVenue Music Audit, $495

h: How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?
t: Each PRO charges separately. ASCAP and BMI base fees mainly on your occupancy and how you use music; SESAC and GMR publish fewer details. On this page What sets the feeASCAP’s 2026 ratesBMI, SESAC and GMRThe totalNext step

The PROs describe broadly similar factors: - How music is used: live, recorded, or audio-visual. ASCAP lists “live, recorded, audio only vs. audio/visual”, the venue’s “capacity”, and “how many nights a week it hosts live music” (ASCAP, why ASCAP licenses bars, restaurants and music venues). - Size. Both ASCAP and BMI tie fees to occupancy; BMI notes occupancy is most commonly set by the local fire marshal (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). - Extras on top of recorded music, such as karaoke and DJs, and any admission or cover charge (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Where you are does not change the ASCAP rate: ASCAP says restaurants of the same size and music use pay the same “regardless of whether the restaurant is in Oshkosh or New York City” (ASCAP).

ASCAP publishes its schedule for restaurants, bars and nightclubs. The annual fee is a rate per occupant, built from the lines below, multiplied by the premises occupancy (if no official occupancy exists, square footage divided by 20). Rates per occupant for calendar year 2026: - Live music, 4 to 7 nights a week : $8.05 - Live music, 3 nights or less : $6.70 - Recorded music, no live music : $4.69 - Recorded music, with live music : $3.10 - Enhancements: karaoke, DJs, emcees, dancing, shows, acts or games : $2.72 - Admission or cover charge : $2.72 - TV or radio only, where the broadcast exemption does not apply : $1.77 The occupancy fee has a minimum of $502, a separate jukebox fee may apply, and the schedule includes adjustments for seasonal venues and an inflation increase each year from 2027. Read the full schedule and its notes before relying on any figure (ASCAP rate schedule and statement of operating policy, calendar year 2026).

- BMI : Says its license “starts at a little more than a dollar per day” and rises with the type of music (recorded, live, DJ, karaoke), how often it is performed, and occupancy (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). - SESAC : Says “music licensing fees vary by industry” and by the degree to which music is used (SESAC, how are fees determined?). - GMR : Says rates “depend upon your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ). We found no published dollar schedule from BMI, SESAC or GMR for bars and restaurants. Ask each for a written quote based on your occupancy and music use.

Because each PRO licenses separately (see Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?), the total depends on how many licenses a venue holds, plus any music service. The National Restaurant Association has said its members pay an average of $4,500 per year to license music (Bloomberg via Indianapolis Business Journal, July 9, 2025). That is an average across members, not a quote for any venue.

h: Music licensing glossary for venue owners
t: The words that come up in PRO letters, rate schedules and music service terms, in plain English. Each entry cites its source and links to the page that explains it. Terms A to Z ABCDEFG H I J K L M N OP Q RS T U V W X Y Z SourcesNext step 20 terms, in alphabetical order. A plain-English summary for general information, not legal advice.

- ASCAP : One of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs). ASCAP says “you need a license with each PRO that represents the creators of the music that you play” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). It publishes a rate schedule for restaurants, bars and nightclubs, with fees per occupant (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- BMI : One of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs). BMI says a license from another PRO “allows you only to perform copyrighted music represented by that organization” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). For bars and restaurants, BMI says its license “starts at a little more than a dollar per day” and rises with the type of music, how often it is performed, and occupancy (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar? - Business music service : A service that licenses the recorded music it supplies for background use in a business, such as Pandora CloudCover, Mood Media, Rockbot or Soundtrack. A service generally covers its own recorded catalog played in public areas, not live performances, cover artists, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). Explained in Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar?; Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke?

- Consent decree : ASCAP and BMI operate under long-standing antitrust consent decrees with the Department of Justice; SESAC and GMR do not. The DOJ notes the decrees “regulate only ASCAP and BMI” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2), and the Copyright Office says “neither SESAC nor GMR is subject to such direct antitrust regulation” (Copyright and the Music Marketplace, p. 34). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR? - Cover charge (Admission charge) : A charge to get in, such as admission or a cover. ASCAP’s 2026 rate schedule adds a line of $2.72 per occupant for an admission or cover charge (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Music services treat it as a limit too: Soundtrack says that if a business “Charges an admission fee”, the public performance rights “are not licensed by Soundtrack” (Soundtrack General Terms), and SESAC says a service’s license “only extends to the music they supply to establishments with no admission, membership or similar charge” (SESAC FAQ). Explained in How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?; Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke?

- Direct PRO license : A license a venue takes from a PRO itself, rather than through a music service. Venues that play music not supplied by a licensed service, or that host live music, DJs or karaoke, may need licenses from each PRO whose catalog is played (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). Explained in Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar?

- Enhancements : The line in ASCAP’s rate schedule for karaoke, DJs, emcees, dancing, shows, acts or games. For 2026 it adds $2.72 per occupant to the annual rate (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Explained in How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- Fractional licensing (Split works) : Songs are often co-written by writers who belong to different PROs: the rights “are often split among multiple songwriters, with differing publishers and PROs” (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015), p. 123). Under fractional licensing a PRO licenses only its share of a work, “meaning that a licensee must obtain a license from all of the PROs affiliated with the work (or from the songwriters or publishers directly) in order to legally perform it” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?

- GMR (Global Music Rights) : Global Music Rights, one of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs). GMR says licenses with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC “do not grant you authorization” to perform music by its writers, “and vice versa”, and that its rates “depend upon your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- Live performance (Live music, DJs and karaoke) : Music performed on the premises by a band, a DJ or karaoke. Each of the four PROs says the license for performances on a venue’s premises is the business’s responsibility, not the performer’s (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, GMR). SESAC puts it as “Paying the band does not cover you” (SESAC FAQ). Business music services generally do not cover live performances (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). Explained in Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke?

- Occupancy : The capacity figure that ASCAP and BMI use to set their fees. BMI notes occupancy is most commonly set by the local fire marshal (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). In ASCAP’s 2026 schedule, the annual fee is a rate per occupant multiplied by the premises occupancy; if no official occupancy exists, square footage divided by 20 (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Explained in How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- Performing rights organization (PRO) : An organization that licenses the public performance of songs for songwriters and publishers. Bars, restaurants and hotels are among the businesses that take PRO licenses (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). The four in the US are ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR. Each represents its own members’ works, so a venue can need more than one license (SESAC, “What is a performing rights organization?”). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; Got a letter from BMI, ASCAP, SESAC or GMR? - Personal streaming account : A consumer plan from a service such as Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube. Their terms limit use to personal listening: Spotify grants permission for “personal, non-commercial use” (Spotify End User Agreement, section 3), and Apple allows use “only for personal, noncommercial purposes” (Apple Media Services Terms, section F). Explained in Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar? - PRO letter : A letter from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC or GMR. A first letter usually offers a license and asks about your venue; some go on to follow-up contact. In October 2026, music publishers and songwriters affiliated with AS

- Repertory search (Songview) : A free search, published by each PRO, that shows which PRO represents a song. Songview is a shared database that BMI describes as covering “the four major PROs, BMI, ASCAP, GMR and SESAC”, with ownership shares per song (Songview at BMI; also reachable from ASCAP’s repertory search). SESAC and GMR publish their own searches (SESAC repertory search, Global Music Rights search). A search tells you who represents a song, not whether your venue is licensed for it. Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?

- SESAC : One of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs). SESAC says each organization “licenses only the copyrighted works of its own respective copyright holders” (SESAC FAQ), and that “music licensing fees vary by industry” and by the degree to which music is used (SESAC, how are fees determined?). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar? - Small-business exemption (17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B)) : A narrow exemption in 17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B) for playing a transmission from an FCC-licensed radio or TV station (or, for video, a cable system or satellite carrier). Food and drink venues under 3,750 gross square feet, and other businesses under 2,000, have no equipment limits; larger venues qualify only within limits on loudspeakers, screens and screen size. Other conditions apply in every case, such as no direct charge to see or hear the transmission (17 U.S.C. §110(5), exemption for certain establishments). It never covers streaming services, downloads, CDs or vinyl, live music, DJs or karaoke, or music added to social media or marketing videos. Explained in Is my venue exempt from music licensing? - Statutory damag

- Willful infringement : Infringement that a court finds willful. US law then allows statutory damages of up to $150,000 per work, above the $750 to $30,000 range that otherwise applies (17 U.S.C. §504(c), statutory damages). The range describes the law, not the likely outcome for any venue. Explained in Got a letter from BMI, ASCAP, SESAC or GMR?

h: Music licensing for hotels: lobby, restaurant, events and rooms
t: A hotel often has many music uses under one roof. Here is what the PROs’ own documents say about each one, use by use. On this page Music in a hotelUse by useHow fees are setNext step

h: Music in a hotel is a public performance
t: US copyright law says a work is performed “publicly” when it is performed “at a place open to the public or at any place where a substantial number of persons outside of a normal circle of a family and its social acquaintances is gathered” (17 U.S.C. §101, definitions). Performing rights organizations (PROs) license that right for songwriters and publishers. SESAC puts it simply for hotels: “If your hotel uses music in guest areas, then you likely need a license” (SESAC, music licensing for hotels). SESAC lists “hotels, motels, resorts, health clubs” among its licensees (SESAC FAQ), and Global Music Rights (GMR) names hotels among the business types it treats differently when setting rates (Global Music Rights FAQ). Each PRO licenses only its own catalog. ASCAP’s hotel license says its fees “specifically exclude the value” of rights controlled by “Broadcast Music, Inc., SESAC Inc. and Global Music Rights” (ASCAP Musical Works License Agreement for Hotels and Motels, 2022 form, published by AHLA). GMR says licenses with the other three “do not grant you authorization” to perform its writers’ music, “and vice versa” (Global Music Rights FAQ). Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR? expl

h: Hotel music uses, one by one
t: ASCAP’s hotel license sets out, area by area, how it treats a hotel. It splits music into “Recorded Music Activity” and “Live Entertainment Activity”, and leaves out “Third-Party Licensable Activity”, which it defines in three parts (ASCAP hotel license, 2022 form). The quotes below come from that form unless another source is named. Other PROs’ licenses and later ASCAP versions may be worded differently. - Lobby and background music : Recorded music is any public performance at the hotel “whether in common areas (including gyms and spas) or Lodging Rooms”, by recordings, digital audio, radio or TV. Music from “any jukebox, background music service” is left out of the hotel license where its public performance is “otherwise licensed or licensable” through ASCAP or the Jukebox License Office. SESAC says a background music service’s license “only extends to the music they supply to establishments with no admission, membership or similar charge” (SESAC FAQ). - Restaurant and bar : An outlet the hotel runs itself is part of the premises the hotel license covers. An area “operated by or predominantly under the control of a third party pursuant to a lease, license or other agreement”, wh

In ASCAP’s 2022 hotel form, the recorded music fee for each hotel follows its number of guest rooms (“Lodging Rooms”), and the live entertainment fee follows what the hotels spend on live entertainment over the year. The license covers only the hotels listed in its Schedule A; the licensee’s other hotels “are not covered by or subject to this License Agreement” (ASCAP hotel license, 2022 form). GMR says its rate depends on “your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ), and SESAC says its fees “are determined by relevant industry criteria” (SESAC FAQ). For a sense of scale, Bloomberg reported this example from the American Hotel & Lodging Association: “A large hotel that hosts occasional live music events could be paying a single PRO $5,000 to $20,000 a year. If it’s paying all of the major PROs, it could be incurring as much as $80,000 in fees, according to the association” (Bloomberg via Indianapolis Business Journal, July 9, 2025). That is the association’s example, not a quote for any hotel. What does a music license cost? covers the fee factors for restaurants and bars.

t: The Venue Music Audit lists each music use in the hotel, from lobby to ballroom, against the licenses you hold, by PRO. For several properties, the Group Audit covers up to 10 venues for $1,950. Free 2-minute checkVenue Music Audit, $495

h: Can my venue use popular songs in Instagram or TikTok videos?
t: Music in a video you post is a different use from music played in the room. The platforms’ own terms set tighter limits for business and promotional posts than for personal ones. On this page A different useWhat the platforms sayCommon optionsNext step

h: A different use from the music in your room
t: The licenses a venue holds for music on its premises are about performing music there. ASCAP’s hotel license, for example, does not grant the right to perform its music “to persons beyond the Premises by any means, methodology or technology”, including “internet-connected websites, software applications, systems, platforms”, and grants no right to “reproduce, copy or distribute” the music or to use the sound recordings (ASCAP Musical Works License Agreement for Hotels and Motels, 2022 form, published by AHLA). Putting a song into a video involves other rights. SESAC explains that it “does not represent the rights needed to reproduce a musical composition into a video”, that “These rights are generally called sync rights”, and that using an existing recording also means contacting “the record label that owns said recording” (SESAC FAQ). On the performance side, SESAC says “Many major social media platforms are already licensed with SESAC” and that it does not usually license “individual users’ channels or pages” (SESAC FAQ). The radio and TV exemption for small venues does not help here either: it never covers music added to social media or marketing videos (Is my venue exempt from

h: What the platforms’ own terms say
t: Each platform sets rules for the music in its own app. These are the platforms’ words about their own services, not a statement of the law. - Facebook and Instagram (Meta) : Meta’s Music Guidelines apply “if you post, share, or promote any videos or other content containing music on any Meta Products”, which include Instagram (Meta Products). They say: “Use of music for commercial or non-personal purposes in particular is prohibited unless you have obtained appropriate licenses”, and “Nothing in these terms constitutes any authorization by us with respect to any use of music” (Meta Music Guidelines, effective March 26, 2024). - Instagram’s music library : “The music available in our library is intended for personal, non-commercial use”, and “certain business accounts and certain types of posts do not have access to the library” (Instagram Help, access to the licensed music library). A reel you boost as an ad “can’t use licensed music”; Instagram recommends “royalty-free music, like what’s available in our Sound Collection, or original audio” (Instagram Help, how to boost a reel). - TikTok : TikTok’s Commercial Music Library is made available to “brands, businesses, commercial entit

General information, not a recommendation for any post. Each option comes with its own terms. - The platform’s commercial library. Instagram says Meta’s Sound Collection has “over 14,000 songs and sounds” and “can be used for commercial purposes like ads” (Instagram Help). TikTok’s Commercial Music Library stays on TikTok: “Commercial Uses outside of TikTok are not permitted and no rights are granted by TikTok for such uses” (TikTok CML terms). A track picked in one app may not cover the same video posted elsewhere. - Music licensed for video. For a specific song, SESAC points to the song’s publishers for sync rights and to the record label for the recording (SESAC FAQ). Music libraries sell licenses too; their terms say which platforms and uses are included. - Original audio. Voice-over, your own sound, or no music at all. Instagram lists original audio as an alternative for boosted reels (Instagram Help). A clip filmed during service also records whatever music is playing in the room. Platform terms change. The versions quoted here were read on November 13, 2026.

Personal Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube accounts are limited by their terms to personal, non-commercial use. Explained in Spotify in a business. - Live music nights: how often, and in which room. Sereinora uses Google OAuth and YouTube API Services to manage Sereinora-controlled YouTube channels. Sereinora uses Google OAuth and YouTube API Services to: - publish Sereinora audiovisual releases that have been explicitly approved for publication; - verify the authorized Sereinora YouTube channel; - retrieve limited information about recent Sereinora YouTube uploads; and - retrieve YouTube Analytics information for Sereinora's own channel and releases. Sereinora currently requests the following Google OAuth permissions: - youtube.upload , to upload approved videos to an authorized YouTube channel; - youtube.readonly , to retrieve authorized YouTube channel and video information; and - yt-analytics.readonly , to retrieve authorized YouTube Analytics information. These permissions are used only for the functionality described above.

Depending on the operation performed, Sereinora may access and locally store: - OAuth authorization credentials; - authorized YouTube channel identity information; - limited recent-upload information, including provider video identifiers, publication dates and privacy states; - YouTube Analytics daily rows and coverage information; and - delivery information needed to verify an authorized upload and prevent duplicate publication. OAuth credentials are stored using secure credential storage controlled by Sereinora. Authorized channel, upload and Analytics information used by Sereinora is stored locally in storage controlled by Sereinora. Sereinora does not request, collect or store your Google or YouTube password.

h: How Google and YouTube Data Is Used
t: Google and YouTube API data is used only to operate Sereinora's authorized YouTube publishing, verification and analytics functionality. Sereinora does not sell Google or YouTube user data. Sereinora does not use Google or YouTube user data for advertising. Sereinora does not transfer Google or YouTube Authorized Data to advertising platforms, data brokers, third-party analytics services, OpenAI, Buffer or unrelated third parties. The Google and YouTube services themselves necessarily receive information required to provide OAuth, YouTube Data API and YouTube Analytics API functionality. Sereinora's use and transfer of information received from Google APIs adheres to the Google API Services User Data Policy, including applicable Limited Use requirements.

Sereinora retains Google and YouTube API data only for as long as required for the authorized operational purpose and in accordance with applicable Google and YouTube API requirements. YouTube Analytics data may be retained while the relevant authorization remains active, subject to the authorization and data-validity checks required by YouTube. Other stored YouTube API data is refreshed or deleted within the periods required by YouTube's Developer Policies. Sereinora does not retain independently calculated metrics derived from YouTube API Data where such derivation is prohibited by YouTube's Developer Policies.

Sereinora provides a Revoke YouTube Access control for its YouTube authorization. Because Google's authorization semantics apply across the relevant Sereinora Google project, using this control revokes Sereinora's YouTube authorization for both publishing and read/Analytics functionality. On successful revocation, Sereinora removes the applicable locally stored OAuth credentials and Authorized Data in accordance with YouTube's requirements. You may also revoke access independently through Google's account security and third-party access settings. Revoking Sereinora's authorization or deleting locally stored Sereinora data does not delete videos or other content stored by YouTube. Content hosted on YouTube must be managed separately through YouTube or another appropriately authorized client.

A user may request deletion of applicable Google or YouTube data stored by Sereinora through Sereinora's deletion controls or by contacting Sereinora. Applicable stored user data will be deleted as soon as possible and within the periods required by YouTube's Developer Policies. Deleting locally stored data does not delete data or videos stored by YouTube.

Sereinora uses technical and operational safeguards appropriate to the data and current use. OAuth credentials are stored using secure credential storage. Publishing credentials and read/Analytics credentials are maintained separately. Sereinora does not intentionally expose Google or YouTube Authorized Data to unrelated external services.

Use of functionality involving YouTube API Services is also subject to YouTube's Terms of Service. Sereinora's use of information received from Google APIs is governed by applicable Google API policies. Google Privacy Policy YouTube Terms of Service
